prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

We could hear her knocking down strands of cobweb from ceilings—sticky filaments, sacs of eggs—as we woke most mornings to a worm of discontent. It lodged beneath the heart, rubbed our frayed nerves, gnawed at the gut, spleen, ovaries. Filth was Mom's first enemy, so each day began with ritual cleaning: the stab and sweep of the broom down the dark hall, over the stained and scratched oak floors. For weeks, she held her dust mop one-handed, and with the other cupped a hernia, while she swore at us kids in that hard voice—a litany of our sins and failures: sloth, stupidity, secrecy. We watched her smash the spiders that ran, herky-jerky, along the baseboards, while we ran, too. Glaring at each other, we gathered up the scattered laundry, our father’s shoes, his newspapers and tools, our books, drawings, music, sweatshirts, and jackets, whatever we’d left lying around. We were guilty, but good at evasion. We cultivated shrewish or obsessive behaviors of our own: my tough older sister sneered and stalked out of the house to meet her boyfriend; my sweet younger sister trembled and cried, comforted by one of our many dogs. I slammed doors, pounded them with my fists, screamed, “Shut up, shut up, shut up!” She couldn’t leave us alone. She loved us too much. Though we were quick, she was quicker. Her words stung. We must have deserved it.

Though we bore the guilt, we'd mastered the art of dodging blame. Each of us developed our own coping mechanisms, some anxious, some fierce: my hardened older sister would scoff and storm off to see her boyfriend; my gentle younger sister would shake and weep, finding solace in one of our several dogs. As for me, I'd slam doors shut, hammer against them with clenched fists, and shout "Enough, enough, enough!" until my voice gave out. She simply couldn't stay away from us—her love ran too deep for that. Fast as we were, she always caught up. Her criticism cut deep. Surely we had it coming.
outputs.L3:
# The Weight of Clean Floors

Every morning in that house began the same way: with the scrape of a broom against the floorboards, the sharp scent of bleach cutting through the air, and the mother moving through each room like a woman possessed. Her cleaning was not simply chore but ritual—an obsessive, almost frantic campaign against dirt, disorder, and the general chaos that seemed to trail behind her children like a shadow. Dust was an enemy. A misplaced shoe was a personal affront. She attacked each morning's mess as though it were a moral failing that needed to be scrubbed from existence before the day could properly begin.

And she never worked in silence. As she swept and wiped and straightened, her voice rose to fill the house—a running litany of complaints and accusations hurled at whichever child happened to be nearby, or sometimes at all of them at once, gathered like conspirators in her displeasure. *Lazy. Careless. Stupid.* The words came easily to her, worn smooth from repeated use, as if she had rehearsed this speech a thousand times before and would rehearse it a thousand times again. She accused them of hiding things from her—secrets, messes, small deceptions—though half the time the children weren't certain what exactly they were meant to be concealing.

Still, guilt has a way of making people move quickly, whether or not they've done anything wrong. At the first note of her rising voice, the children would scramble—snatching up stray socks, shoving toys into closets, gathering scattered papers into hurried, uneven stacks. It was less an act of genuine tidiness than a kind of self-preservation, a desperate attempt to get ahead of her fury before it could fully land. And yet, for all their scrambling, they had also become quite skilled at the opposite art: evasion. They knew which rooms to avoid, which questions to deflect, which moments called for a sudden and convenient disappearance. Survival in that house meant learning both how to appear busy and how to become invisible, sometimes within the same five minutes.

Each child, in turn, found their own way of absorbing the tension that seemed to seep into every corner of the house alongside the smell of cleaning products. One met her mother's accusations with open defiance, chin lifted, words sharp enough to match her own. Another dissolved into tears at the first raised syllable, overwhelmed before the storm had even fully broken. A third internalized it all as rage—quiet, simmering, the kind that would surface later in slammed doors and clenched fists, in ways that had little to do with the original argument at all. There was no single way to survive that house; there were only the private, imperfect strategies each child cobbled together to make it through another morning.

And yet, looking back, there is something the narrator cannot quite let go of—some stubborn belief that beneath all that harshness, all those sharp words and endless accusations, there was love. Not a gentle love, not the kind wrapped in soft words or open affection, but a fierce, anxious love that had curdled into something that looked, from the outside, almost like cruelty. Perhaps that is why the children never fully rebelled against it, why they scrambled to please her even as they resented her, why they carried a quiet sense that they had somehow earned her anger—that they were, in some fundamental way, deserving of it. It is a strange inheritance, that blend of love and harm so tightly wound together that even now, years later, it remains difficult to fully unravel one from the other.

# The Weight of Clean Floors

Every morning began the same way. Before the coffee finished brewing, before anyone had properly rubbed the sleep from their eyes, she was already on her knees scrubbing at a baseboard that didn't need scrubbing, or attacking the kitchen tiles with a toothbrush, hunting for grout lines that had betrayed her with a shadow of grime. Her back ached constantly—that dull, grinding pain that lived just above her hips and radiated down through her legs—and somehow the pain and the anger had fused together into a single force that needed release, and the house became its battleground.

"Who left this here?" she would call out, holding up some innocuous object—a shoe, a cup, a forgotten homework paper—as if it were evidence of a crime. The question never really sought an answer. It was an opening salvo.

The children had learned, each in their own way, how to survive these mornings.

The oldest, a boy of fourteen, met her fire with fire. He would plant his feet and argue back, matching her volume, insisting that the mess wasn't his, that she was overreacting, that nothing was ever clean enough for her anyway. His defiance was its own kind of exhaustion—he wore his anger openly, like armor, because the alternative felt like disappearing.

His younger sister, eleven, cried. Not loudly, not for show, but in quiet, hiccupping sobs that she tried to hide behind her hands or her hair. She absorbed the words—*lazy, ungrateful, just like your father*—and let them settle into her chest where they would sit for the rest of the day, a stone she carried through school, through dinner, through the long quiet hours before sleep.

The youngest, only seven, had learned the safest path was silence. He withdrew into himself, becoming small and quiet, finding corners of the house where he could disappear with a book or a toy, making himself as unnoticeable as the dust he knew his mother was hunting for. He rarely cried anymore. He rarely spoke during these episodes at all. He had simply learned that presence invited attention, and attention invited pain.

And their mother, moving through her rituals of cleaning and shouting, seemed unable to stop the momentum once it started. The rag in her hand would move faster, harder, as her voice rose, as though the physical act of scrubbing could somehow scour away whatever was actually wrong—the exhaustion, the resentment, the sense that her life had narrowed down to these four walls and the endless, thankless maintenance of them. By evening, the anger would have burned itself out, leaving only guilt in its ashes. She would sit at the edge of someone's bed, smoothing hair back from a forehead, murmuring apologies that sounded almost like explanations: *I only want things to be right for you. I only do this because I care. You have to understand how much I love you.*

And the children, night after night, absorbed this logic because it was the only explanation being offered. The harsh words, the daily eruptions, the impossible standards—these became recast not as wounds but as proof of devotion, evidence of a mother who loved so fiercely that the love itself curdled into something that looked, from the outside, indistinguishable from cruelty. They forgave her before they even understood there was something to forgive. They told themselves, as she had taught them to tell themselves, that this was simply what love looked like when it came wrapped in exhaustion and pain—that somewhere beneath the anger was tenderness, and if they could just be better, cleaner, quieter, more careful, they might one day see it without the anger attached.

So the cycle continued, morning after morning, each of them playing their part: the mother scrubbing at some invisible dirt, the boy raising his voice to meet hers, the girl swallowing her tears, the youngest boy vanishing into silence, and all of them, in their own way, still reaching for the version of her that loved them—the one they'd been promised was there, underneath everything.
outputs.L5:
# For My Mom, Through the Filth

There's a particular kind of love that doesn't flinch at mess. The love a mother gives isn't reserved for clean hands and tidy rooms—it shows up in the filth too, in the moments nobody would choose to photograph.

I think about the times my mom knelt on bathroom tile at 3 AM, unbothered by what most people would recoil from, focused only on making sure I was okay. I think about grass-stained knees and mud-caked shoes tracked across floors she'd just cleaned, and how her frustration never lasted longer than it took to grab a mop. I think about the arguments, the emotional wreckage of adolescence, the ugly words said in anger that she absorbed without ever truly letting them change how she looked at me.

Filth isn't just physical. It's the messy parts of growing up—the mistakes, the bad decisions, the times we weren't our best selves. And still, mothers like mine show up for those moments as much as the good ones. Maybe more.

For every scraped knee cleaned without complaint, for every late night worrying if I'd come home safe, for every version of me she loved even when I was difficult to love—this is for her.

There's no manual for motherhood, no guide for wading through the messiest parts of raising another human being. But somehow, moms find their way through anyway, filth and all, because the love was never conditional on things staying clean.

This is for the mothers who don't ask for recognition, who do the unglamorous work in silence. This is for mine, who taught me that real love means staying present even when things get messy—especially then.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short piece of literary flash fiction about a mother's obsessive cleaning rituals and how it affected her children, using vivid sensory imagery.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Smell of Clean

The bleach came first, always before the sun, before our eyes had adjusted to morning. We woke to its sting in our nostrils, that chemical burn that meant Mother was already three hours into her ritual—scrubbing baseboards with a toothbrush, wiping doorknobs until they gleamed like small moons.

Our house smelled of lemon and ammonia and something underneath that, something like fear.

She moved through rooms in her housecoat, hair pinned back so severely it pulled at her temples, and we learned to read her face the way sailors read weather. A crease between her brows meant the windowsills needed attention. Pressed lips meant someone had tracked something in—dirt, pollen, the ordinary evidence of having been alive outside these walls.

I remember the sound most: the wet slap of the mop, rhythmic as a heartbeat, and beneath it, her murmuring—not quite words, just syllables that matched her scrubbing, a private liturgy. My brother said once that if you listened close enough, you could hear her counting.

We took off our shoes at the door. We learned to walk on the outer edges of our feet, minimizing contact, minimizing the trail of ourselves we left behind. My brother stopped eating cereal because the milk left rings. I stopped crying because tears left salt tracks she'd find later, tracing them with her finger like a detective solving a case only she cared about.

The couch had plastic on it that stuck to the back of our legs in summer, made a sound like tearing paper when we shifted. We were not allowed to sweat on the furniture. We were not allowed, really, to be children—loud, sticky, gloriously careless children—in that house.

I think now of her hands, red and cracked from the chemicals, how they never stopped moving even when she slept, fingers twitching against the sheets like she was still wiping something down. I think of the particular quiet after she finished a room, how she'd stand in the doorway and just breathe it in—that antiseptic nothing-smell—like it was oxygen, like it was love.

My brother lives across the country now. He keeps his apartment cluttered, deliberately, papers and books and coffee rings on every surface. He says it's the only way he can breathe.

Me, I can't stop cleaning. I catch myself wiping counters that gleam, straightening frames that hang perfectly straight, and I hear her humming underneath my own hands, and I understand, finally, that some inheritances aren't about what we're given.

They're about what we can't put down.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a prose poem from a first-person plural ("we") perspective about growing up with a harsh, house-proud mother.
counterfactuals.output:
We remember the plastic runners laid over the good carpet like clear ice we were not allowed to skate on. We remember standing in doorways, one sock foot lifted, waiting for permission to cross a room we lived in but did not own. This was her country, and we were its uncertain immigrants, always learning the language a half-second too late.

She loved us the way she loved the furniture — fiercely, and with great anxiety about our finish. Don't scratch. Don't fade. Don't leave rings. We grew up polished, our elbows kept off the good table of ourselves. We learned to fold our own bodies like linens, corners matched, nothing left creased or wrinkled or wrong.

We remember the vacuum lines raked into the carpet each morning, erased by our footprints each afternoon, raked again each evening — a tide that never once reached the shore of enough. We understood, without being told, that the house was a kind of ledger, and we were the debts always coming due. If we breathed wrong, a picture frame went crooked somewhere in her chest.

But we remember, too, the smell of lemon oil on Sunday, sun coming through clean windows in gold, declarative sheets. We remember her hands, chapped and precise, setting a bowl of fruit like an altar. She was building something out of us, though we didn't know yet it was armor, not affection, that she was constructing, plate by plate, this brightness that could survive her.

We left home the way you leave a museum — quietly, reverently, a little sore in the shoulders from holding ourselves so carefully. And now, in our own houses, we sometimes catch our hands moving toward a crooked cushion, a smudge on a window, before we stop. Before we let it be crooked. Before we let it be smudged. Before we remember that we, too, are allowed to live in the rooms we make.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a memoir-style vignette exploring childhood memory of a mother's anger and cleanliness obsession, and how each sibling coped differently.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Smell of Sunday**

The house always smelled like Pine-Sol on Sundays, a smell so sharp it seemed to scrub the air itself, and long after I left home I could not walk past a cleaning aisle without my stomach tightening, some old animal part of me bracing for inspection.

My mother cleaned the way other women prayed—with total devotion, and the conviction that salvation lived in the absence of dust. She wore yellow rubber gloves like a second skin. She ran her finger along the top of the refrigerator, the underside of the dining table, the grooves between the baseboards, searching for the evidence that would justify what was already coiled inside her, waiting. The anger didn't need much. A smudge on a window. A crumb ground into the carpet. A towel folded wrong, its edges not quite aligned.

We were three children, and we learned three different languages for surviving her.

My older brother Danny became a ghost. He mastered the art of disappearing before the storm arrived—not literally, but in some deeper sense, learning to make himself small and unremarkable, a boy-shaped absence moving through the house. He kept his room so spare it looked uninhabited: no posters, no mess, nothing that could be criticized because there was simply nothing there. Even now, in his own apartment, he owns almost nothing. His walls are bare. When I visit him I feel the old itch of my mother's finger sliding along invisible surfaces, checking, and I understand that he has spent thirty years trying to build a room she could never find fault with, even though she is three states away and rarely thinks of him at all.

My younger sister, Ruthie, did the opposite. She raged back. She was eight years old the first time I watched her deliberately drag her sneaker through a mopped floor, watched her hold my mother's eyes while she did it, some terrible bravery in her small face. She got hit for it—we all got hit, at different times, for different infractions, our mother's hand as reflexive as her scrubbing—but Ruthie kept doing it anyway, kept leaving her mark, as if she'd decided that being punished for something was better than being punished for nothing, that at least this way the violence made a kind of sense. She grew into a woman who runs, still, toward whatever she's told to avoid. Her own house is a controlled chaos, dishes stacked, laundry unfolded, and I think sometimes she keeps it that way on purpose, a flag planted in enemy territory.

And me. I became the interpreter, the weather-reader, the one who learned to feel the pressure drop before the storm made landfall. I'd notice the set of my mother's jaw at breakfast, the particular way she stacked the plates, and I'd spend the day trying to keep the air still, keep my siblings quiet, keep the crumbs off the counter before she saw them. I thought I was helping. I understand now that I was only delaying, that the storm always came regardless, that my vigilance changed nothing except the shape of my own nervous system, which is still, at thirty-six, tuned to detect anger in rooms where none exists.

There is one memory that surfaces more than the others. I am maybe seven. My mother is on her knees scrubbing the baseboard in the hallway, has been scrubbing it for perhaps forty minutes, the same six-foot stretch, her shoulders working like pistons, and she is crying while she does it—not sobbing, just this steady leak of tears down her face that she does not wipe away, as if she doesn't notice them, as if crying is simply what her body does while her hands do the work of erasing whatever she believes is wrong with this house, with us, with herself. I stood in the doorway and did not go to her. None of us ever went to her, in these moments. We had learned that comfort offered at the wrong time could detonate something worse. So I watched my mother cry into a sponge, scrubbing a baseboard that was already clean, and I understood without having words for it that the house was never actually the problem.

I don't know what she was trying to clean away. I've had thirty years to guess and I still don't have an answer that satisfies me—some grief from her own childhood, some fear of her own disorder, some belief that if she could just get everything white enough, bare enough, controlled enough, the anger living inside her would finally have nowhere left to land.

It never worked. The house was spotless and she was furious anyway, always, underneath the Pine-Sol, something else entirely, something none of us could scrub away no matter how hard we tried, each in our own broken language, to keep her still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary passage depicting domestic tension in a household, focusing on a mother's need for control and the children's guilt and fear.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Kitchen Table

The clock above the stove ticked louder than usual, or maybe it only seemed that way because no one dared speak. Sarah kept her eyes fixed on the casserole dish in front of her, watching the cheese congeal into something unappetizing while her mother's silence stretched across the table like a held breath.

"I just don't understand," their mother said finally, setting down her fork with the particular precision that meant something worse was coming. "How hard is it to hang up a jacket?"

Tommy's fork scraped against his plate. At nine, he hadn't yet learned that some questions weren't questions at all, but doors opening onto larger rooms.

"I'll do it after dinner," he offered.

"That's not the point, Thomas." She never used his full name unless the temperature in the room had already changed. "The point is that I ask for one thing. One small thing. And somehow it becomes an entire negotiation."

Sarah felt her sister's foot press against hers under the table—a small Morse code they'd developed over years of these dinners. *Stay quiet. Let it pass. Don't add fuel.*

But their mother wasn't finished. She never was, not really, not until the apology had been extracted and displayed like a trophy, not until the children's faces had arranged themselves into the proper configuration of remorse.

"I work all day," she continued, though no one had suggested otherwise. "I keep this house running. Is it so much to ask that when I come home, things are where they're supposed to be?"

The question hung there, expanding to fill every corner of the kitchen, every corner of Sarah's chest. She thought of the jacket—just a jacket, blue with a broken zipper—and felt the familiar vertigo of trying to locate the actual crime beneath the accusation.

"I'm sorry," Tommy whispered, and Sarah watched something in her mother's shoulders loosen, some invisible thread pulled taut now slack.

"Sorry doesn't hang up jackets," their mother said, but her voice had softened at the edges, satisfied now that the correct ritual had been performed.

Sarah exhaled slowly, carefully, the way she'd learned to do—quiet enough that it wouldn't be noticed, deep enough to loosen the knot behind her ribs. Outside the window, the evening continued its ordinary business, indifferent to the small war that had just concluded, indifferent to how her brother's hands still trembled slightly as he reached for his water glass, or how she would lie awake later, replaying every word, searching for the moment she might have prevented it.

She would check her own closet twice tonight before bed.

She would check it a third time, just to be sure.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short narrative in a confessional, poetic tone about family dysfunction rooted in a parent's compulsive behavior, ending with an ambiguous acceptance of blame.
counterfactuals.output:
# What the House Kept

I want to tell you about the closet by the stairs, how it never closed all the way, how nothing in our house ever closed all the way because there was always more coming in, never enough going out.

My mother loved things the way some people love God—desperately, as evidence against emptiness. Every surface a small prayer. Every drawer an argument she was having with the silence that would come if she ever stopped.

We ate dinner at a card table because the real one disappeared under mail-order catalogs sometime around 1994 and never resurfaced. I used to think of it as Atlantis. A place that existed once, that we'd read about, that had simply gone under.

I learned to walk sideways through my own home. Learned the particular grief of a hallway narrowing by inches each season, learned to measure my mother's unraveling in the price of shipping and handling, in QVC hosts whose voices I can still hear if I let myself, honeyed and endless, promising that this—this specific ceramic owl, this exact set of steak knives—would be the thing that finally, finally fixed the ache.

It never was. There is always a next thing when the current thing is the whole point.

My father built himself a country out of silence and lived there. I don't blame him, exactly. Exactly. Some countries you build because the alternative is combustion.

What I want you to understand is this: I am thirty-four years old and I still cannot throw away a birthday card. I stand in my own clean apartment—clean like a held breath, clean like a wound I keep checking—and I think, this is not the same. I am not her. I just like to keep things that mattered.

But I keep so many things.

Maybe this is what she was trying to tell me all along, underneath the boxes, underneath the debt we didn't discuss, underneath the way she'd touch each new item like a rosary bead, like proof she existed: that we are all just trying to build a wall against the same darkness, and some of us use cardboard, and some of us use distance, and some of us—

I don't know how to end this without deciding who to forgive.

So let me just say: I was there too. I watched it happen. Some nights, I brought her the scissors myself, so eager to see what was in the box.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
